lesson_title: The Supplier Says You Owe More: Reconciliations
hook_text: Their statement says R52 900. Your book says R33 400. Skip the check and you pay R13 700 too much.
clip_script: Month-end. Siyakha Wholesalers sends a statement: you owe fifty-two thousand nine hundred. Your own book says thirty-three thousand four hundred. Before anyone shouts — sit down and take the differences one by one, because each belongs to somebody. Their statement has an invoice for five thousand eight hundred: the goods really arrived on the thirtieth, so YOUR book is behind — it catches up. You paid seven thousand six hundred on the twenty-ninth; their statement was printed on the twenty-sixth — their side comes down. The eight-fifty discount they promised isn't processed yet — down again. The damaged goods you returned — down again. And then the gem: an invoice for three thousand five hundred that is not yours at all. Somebody at Siyakha posted another customer's shopping to YOUR account. Down once more. Now both records say the same thing: thirty-nine thousand two hundred. THAT is what you pay. Count what twenty minutes of checking was worth: pay the raw statement and you throw away thirteen thousand seven hundred rand — including someone else's groceries. And here is the dangerous part: fake invoices flow toward businesses that never check, because word gets around about who pays blind. So the rule is one sentence long. Never pay a statement. Pay a RECONCILED statement.
visual_style: Two paper columns facing each other like duelling receipts, line items sliding down or across as each difference finds its owner; the wrong-customer invoice glowing red before it drops; both columns clicking to the same total.
pacing: Confrontational open, rhythmic item-by-item beats, slow reveal on the stranger's invoice, punchy one-line rule to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and reconcile any statement, bank account or debtors' book a question sets.
